ReTouchGS: Ultralight Render-free Aesthetic Color Enhancement and Transfer for 3D Gaussian Splatting

Chuanzhi Xu    Boyu Wei    Chengkun Yue Affiliation: The University of Sydney Indiana University  Project Page    Xuanhua Yin    Yiyang Li    Haodong Chen    Qiang Qu    Weidong Cai
Abstract

3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables photorealistic scene reconstruction. Existing 3DGS color transfer and interactive editing methods are guided by reference images and user-specified color adjustments. However, in many applications, users simply want aesthetically guided color enhancement that automatically makes the scene more visually appealing while maintaining consistent colors and tones across viewpoints. We present ReTouchGS, to our knowledge the first framework for reference-free aesthetic color enhancement of pretrained 3DGS models. It predicts a scene-level color lookup table (LUT) from the model and its associated camera parameters. ReTouchGS also supports reference-guided color transfer by fitting a scene-level LUT using one edited view of the same scene and its corresponding original render. A shared blend-aware color refinement network with only 44.7K parameters refines an analytic color update to realize either color mapping without rendering. It preserves geometry and delivers standard 3DGS assets in seconds. We also design the ReTouch3D benchmark to support the evaluation of aesthetic color enhancement and reference-guided color transfer across viewpoints. Experiments demonstrate high color accuracy and strong generalization to unseen scenes in both aesthetic color enhancement and reference-guided color transfer.

1 Introduction

3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [11] enables photorealistic reconstruction and real-time rendering of reusable scene assets. As these assets support immersive viewing and visual creation, their aesthetic appeal becomes increasingly important. Adjusting a scene’s exposure, color balance, and tone can improve its overall aesthetic presentation. Therefore, creators need tools that automatically enhance scene colors or transfer preferred colors and tones from an edited view, with consistent results across viewpoints (Figure 1).

In 2D photography, learning from expert retouching provides a foundation for automatic aesthetic enhancement. Datasets such as MIT-Adobe FiveK [2] and PPR10K [15] pair photographs with expert edits, making photographic aesthetic preferences available for learning. Image enhancement methods learn these preferences through image-adaptive lookup tables (LUTs) [30, 28, 29] and color-aware tone curves [21], adjusting color and tone based on image content to improve aesthetic presentation. Users may also want to bring these aesthetic enhancements to 3D scenes.

Several studies support 3D appearance editing guided by reference images or user input. Reference-guided color transfer [24, 26] propagates adjustments from a retouched view, and interactive editing [4] provides palette and luminance controls. Similarly, reference-based stylization [12, 33] transfers a chosen visual style. However, users often seek a more visually appealing scene without having a reference image or a specific set of color adjustments in mind. Meeting this need requires automatic, reference-free aesthetic color enhancement of pretrained 3DGS assets, a task that existing work has not addressed.

Extending aesthetic enhancement to 3DGS presents three challenges. First, image-adaptive enhancement applied independently to each view can produce different colors and tones [26], requiring a consistent retouching decision for the whole scene. Second, preserving the retouched appearance in the model for subsequent novel-view rendering requires faithfully encoding this decision in Gaussian color parameters. However, the order of nonlinear color transformation and Gaussian blending affects the resulting pixel colors, so directly transforming each Gaussian’s color produces discrepancies with the target pixel colors. Third, rendering-based editing [24, 3] repeatedly renders the scene during per-scene optimization, adding substantial computation even for color adjustments. Such optimization must also preserve the reconstructed geometry and view-dependent appearance to avoid structural or appearance artifacts. These requirements motivate render-free color updates that preserve geometry and opacity.

In this paper, we propose ReTouchGS, to our knowledge the first framework for reference-free aesthetic color enhancement of pretrained 3DGS assets, and it also supports reference-guided color transfer. For reference-free enhancement, an aesthetic enhancement network learns from an image enhancer trained on expert-retouched photographs and predicts a scene-level LUT from the asset and its associated camera parameters. The resulting RGB-to-RGB mapping is shared across viewpoints of the 3DGS scene. For color transfer, we instead fit this mapping to a user-edited view and its corresponding original render. Both tasks use a shared render-free color update stage that combines an analytic color update with learned color corrections from the blend-aware color refinement network, preserving geometry and opacity in a standard 3DGS asset. The framework uses only 180.2K network parameters for reference-free enhancement and 44.7K for color transfer.

We also introduce the ReTouch3D benchmark with scene-consistent color targets for 37 scenes. ReTouchGS delivers retouched assets in seconds and achieves mean color errors of 5.50 Δ​E76\Delta E_{76} for aesthetic enhancement and 4.03 Δ​E76\Delta E_{76} for reference-guided color transfer on views beyond the capture trajectory. It outperforms all baselines in color accuracy, PSNR, and LPIPS on both tasks.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    We propose ReTouchGS, the first framework, to our knowledge, for reference-free aesthetic color enhancement of pretrained 3DGS assets, with support for reference-guided color transfer.

  • •

    We introduce the ReTouch3D benchmark with scene-consistent color targets and off-trajectory evaluation of retouching fidelity and cross-view generalization.

  • •

    We develop a shared blend-aware color refinement network that refines analytic color updates to embed predicted or reference-fitted color mappings in standard Gaussian assets without rendering. Experiments show that ReTouchGS outperforms all evaluated baselines in color accuracy, PSNR, and LPIPS on both tasks.

2 Related Work

2D Image Aesthetic Enhancement. Expert-retouched datasets [2, 15] support learning aesthetic color and tonal adjustments for 2D photographs. Image-adaptive 3D LUTs [30] represent these adjustments by combining learned basis tables. AdaInt [28] adapts their color-space sampling, while SepLUT [29] separates channel-independent adjustments from channel interactions. NamedCurves [21] learns tone curves for named colors and combines the adjusted images through attention. These methods establish strong photographic retouching priors at the image level. ReTouchGS brings the learned aesthetic decision to a pretrained 3DGS asset, predicting scene-wide colors and tones and embedding them in Gaussian colors for consistent novel-view rendering.

3D Color Editing and Transfer. BilaRF [24] and Xiao et al. [26] propagate enhancement from an edited view to neural radiance fields and 3DGS, respectively. IReNe [19] and VIRGi [20] support user-directed recoloring while preserving view-dependent effects, and ReparamGS [4] provides interactive palette and luminance controls. Instant Colorization [16] and Support-Aware Appearance Distillation (SAAD) [3] fit Gaussian colors to edited targets through visibility-weighted least squares and spherical harmonic distillation, respectively. FPGS [12] and StyleMe3D [33] transfer reference styles to Gaussian scenes, with StyleMe3D incorporating perceptual quality priors. ViP3DE [5] uses video priors for multi-view consistent editing. Rendering-based optimization methods, such as BilaRF [24] and SAAD [3], repeatedly render the scene during editing, adding computational overhead even for color adjustments. However, these methods require users to specify the target appearance through reference examples or interactive controls. Luminance-GS [7] and LITA-GS [32] address reconstruction under challenging illumination, restoring scene appearance from degraded observations. In contrast, ReTouchGS automatically determines how to improve a pretrained 3DGS scene’s existing colors based on aesthetic criteria without a reference, and efficiently realizes that decision through render-free color updates that preserve geometry and opacity. The same LUT representation and color refinement network also support reference-guided color transfer.

3 ReTouch3D Benchmark

Paired 3D scenes with view-consistent photographic retouching targets are scarce. We construct ReTouch3D to support the evaluation of 3D aesthetic color enhancement and reference-guided color transfer using scene-consistent targets derived from expert retouching priors (Figure 2).

The benchmark evaluates two tasks on 3D scenes: reference-free aesthetic color enhancement and reference-guided color transfer. Reference-free aesthetic color enhancement takes a 3D asset 𝒢s\mathcal{G}_{s} and its associated camera parameters 𝒞s\mathcal{C}_{s}, including intrinsics and poses, and predicts aesthetically enhanced colors and tones using learned photographic retouching priors. Reference-guided color transfer additionally receives one edited view of the same scene at reference viewpoint v0v_{0}, to specify the preferred colors and tones. In both tasks, ReTouchGS outputs a retouched standard 3DGS asset whose novel views express the desired colors and tones. The two tasks share the same target colors and tones, along with the evaluation views.

3.1 Aesthetic Target Construction

An image enhancer generates aesthetic targets from original renders at reconstruction viewpoints. We use NamedCurves MIT5K-DPE [21], trained on expert edits from MIT-Adobe FiveK [2]. The image enhancer independently adjusts colors and tones according to the content visible in each view, which can lead to cross-view inconsistencies. Therefore, we jointly fit one scene-level RGB grid LUT to multiple enhanced reconstruction views to establish a consistent color mapping for the entire scene. Pooling views exposes the fit to different scene regions and color distributions. Let TsT_{s} denote the fitted operator, RR the 3DGS renderer, and Π\Pi clipping to [0,1][0,1]. The target at any viewpoint vv is:

Is⋆​(v)=Ts​(Π⁡(R⁡(𝒢s,v))).I_{s}^{\star}(v)=T_{s}\!\left(\Pi(R(\mathcal{G}_{s},v))\right). (1)

This shared operator fixes the color mapping across viewpoints. Targets are constructed offline, and the evaluator stores the scene LUT and all target images except the supplied edited reference image. Appendix A specifies sampling, fitting, and quantization.

3.2 Evaluation Protocol

ReTouch3D contains 28 test scenes from DL3DV [17] and all nine from Mip-NeRF 360 [1]. Input and held-out reconstruction views are separated. A reusable asset must also preserve the chosen colors and tones when visibility and Gaussian blending change beyond the capture trajectory. Therefore, the primary evaluation uses 16 off-trajectory views per scene, measuring mean pixelwise Δ​E76\Delta E_{76} in CIELAB [10] against the scene-consistent targets. Scores first average views within a scene, then weight all 37 scenes equally. Appendix A provides scene statistics, evaluation-view construction, and metric definitions.

4 Methodology - ReTouchGS

ReTouchGS separates the choice of a scene’s colors and tones from their realization in Gaussian color parameters (Figure 3). Given an asset 𝒢\mathcal{G} and its associated camera parameters 𝒞\mathcal{C}, an aesthetic enhancement network predicts a scene-level color operator for reference-free enhancement. For reference-guided color transfer, the operator is fitted to an edited view and its original render. Both operators enter a shared render-free color update stage. An analytic color update provides an initial transformation, and a blend-aware color refinement network predicts color corrections to produce an edited asset 𝒢′\mathcal{G}^{\prime}. This separation lets learned aesthetic preferences and user-specified colors and tones share one mechanism for consistent 3D retouching.

4.1 Scene-Level Color Operators

A scene-level color operator should apply the same photographic adjustment to corresponding colors across views. We represent this adjustment by a color operator TΘT_{\Theta}. We use grid LUTs by default, predicted for enhancement and fitted to a reference pair for transfer. A uniform RGB grid stores displacements from identity:

TΘ​(x)=Π⁡(x+w​(x)⊤​Θ),T_{\Theta}(x)=\Pi\!\left(x+w(x)^{\top}\Theta\right), (2)

where Θ∈ℝD×3\Theta\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times 3} stores DD LUT-node displacements, w⁡(x)w(x) contains trilinear interpolation weights, and Π\Pi clamps RGB values to [0,1][0,1]. This representation couples color and tonal adjustments in one mapping and provides an explicit zero-edit state at Θ=0\Theta=0.

Reference-Free Aesthetic Color Enhancement. Choosing an aesthetic adjustment requires both the spatial appearance of a scene and its overall color distribution. Our aesthetic enhancement network EϕE_{\phi} obtains these complementary cues by projecting Gaussian centers into coarse image-plane projection grids. It encodes view-dependent spherical harmonic (SH) colors, opacity, and relative scales, then pools features with opacity and depth weights. A convolutional encoder summarizes the resulting spatial features, while RGB and luma quantiles describe the projected color and tonal distribution. A feature encoder combines these cues at each viewpoint, and mean pooling across viewpoints forms one scene descriptor.

Expert-derived scene LUTs contain recurring, correlated photographic adjustments. Therefore, principal component analysis (PCA) of the training LUTs defines a compact space for predicting these adjustments. The network predicts standardized coefficients and reconstructs the LUT as:

zϕ\displaystyle z_{\phi} =Eϕ​(𝒢,𝒞),\displaystyle=E_{\phi}(\mathcal{G},\mathcal{C}), (3)
vec⁡(Θ^)\displaystyle\operatorname{vec}(\widehat{\Theta}) =μ+B⁡(σ⊙zϕ),\displaystyle=\mu+B(\sigma\odot z_{\phi}),

where μ\mu is the mean training LUT, the columns of BB are its principal directions, and σ\sigma contains coefficient standard deviations. Appendix B details the projection and feature construction.

Reference-Guided Color Transfer. An edited view specifies the creator’s preferred colors and tones through corresponding original and target colors. The original asset is rendered once from the reference viewpoint, and a grid LUT is fitted to the paired original and edited RGB values. An identity-centered ridge penalty anchors colors sparsely represented in the reference, allowing one edited view to specify a scene-level mapping. The fitted LUT enters the shared render-free color update stage. The fitting objective and solver settings are specified in Appendix B.

4.2 Blended Color Context and Analytic Color Update

With geometry and opacity fixed, rendered pixels combine contributions from several Gaussians. However, applying a nonlinear operator to this mixture differs from mixing individually transformed colors. Therefore, each Gaussian’s update should account for the colors it contributes to forming. The blended color context mim_{i} is estimated by pooling view-dependent SH colors in coarse projection grids with opacity and soft depth weights, then aggregating the grid colors at Gaussian ii’s projections across viewpoints. This supplies a color around which to approximate the input color transformation using asset attributes and camera projections.

Let cic_{i} be Gaussian ii’s view-independent (DC) color represented by the zeroth-order SH coefficient, hi​ℓh_{i\ell} its higher-order SH coefficients, and ui=Π⁡(ci)u_{i}=\Pi(c_{i}). A first-order expansion of TT around mim_{i} uses the Jacobian JT​(mi)J_{T}(m_{i}). The context weight aia_{i} decreases as the Gaussian’s own color departs from its context, transitioning toward an update at uiu_{i}. The resulting analytic color update is:

ai\displaystyle a_{i} =exp⁡(−‖ci−mi‖22δ2),\displaystyle=\exp\!\left(-\frac{\|c_{i}-m_{i}\|_{2}^{2}}{\delta^{2}}\right), (4)
cicf\displaystyle c_{i}^{\mathrm{cf}} =ai​[T⁡(mi)+JT​(mi)​(ci−mi)]\displaystyle=a_{i}\bigl[T(m_{i})+J_{T}(m_{i})(c_{i}-m_{i})\bigr]
+(1−ai)​[T⁡(ui)+ci−ui],\displaystyle+(1-a_{i})\bigl[T(u_{i})+c_{i}-u_{i}\bigr],
hi​ℓcf\displaystyle h_{i\ell}^{\mathrm{cf}} =[ai​JT​(mi)+(1−ai)​JT​(ui)]​hi​ℓ,\displaystyle=\bigl[a_{i}J_{T}(m_{i})+(1-a_{i})J_{T}(u_{i})\bigr]h_{i\ell},

where ℓ>0\ell>0 and δ\delta controls the decay of the context weight. The DC update changes the base color, while the local Jacobian transforms higher-order SH coefficients so that view-dependent variations follow the same adjustment. The term ci−uic_{i}-u_{i} preserves the DC component outside the LUT domain.

4.3 Blend-Aware Color Refinement Network

The analytic color update captures a local first-order transformation. To account for operator curvature and the approximation of blended color context, the network learns a DC correction through residual propagation between nearby Gaussians. This formulation makes the desired color changes explicit and lets the network learn how to distribute them.

Operator Residuals and Blending Discrepancy Features. Three operator residuals describe direct color displacement, context displacement, and the linearized change in the Gaussian-to-context color difference:

ridir\displaystyle r_{i}^{\mathrm{dir}} =T⁡(ui)−ui,\displaystyle=T(u_{i})-u_{i}, (5)
rictx\displaystyle r_{i}^{\mathrm{ctx}} =T⁡(mi)−mi,\displaystyle=T(m_{i})-m_{i},
rijac\displaystyle r_{i}^{\mathrm{jac}} =JT​(mi)−I~​(c~i−mi).\displaystyle=\widetilde{J_{T}(m_{i})-I}\,(\tilde{c}_{i}-m_{i}).

The matrix II is the 3×33\times 3 identity, and the tildes denote bounded features used in the learned correction, with their ranges specified in Section B.3. To expose the mixing discrepancy directly, a blending discrepancy feature is defined as:

bT​(a,b)=T⁡(a+b2)−T⁡(a)+T⁡(b)2.b_{T}(a,b)=T\!\left(\frac{a+b}{2}\right)-\frac{T(a)+T(b)}{2}. (6)

This blending discrepancy feature measures the difference between transforming a mixture and mixing its transformed colors. Each node uses bT​(ui,mi)b_{T}(u_{i},m_{i}), and each edge uses bT​(ui,uj)b_{T}(u_{i},u_{j}). These LUT queries expose color-space curvature beyond the analytic color update.

Residual Propagation. A 3D nearest-neighbor graph propagates color corrections across local Gaussian neighborhoods. Node and edge features encode Gaussian appearance, blended color context, and relative geometry. These asset-derived features predict scalar propagation coefficients shared by the three RGB channels. The input color operator supplies the residual channels, allowing the same network to handle different color and tonal adjustments.

The network has two residual-propagation layers. The second layer appends first-layer corrections to its node and neighbor residuals, allowing neighboring corrections to inform the final update. Let 𝒩+​(i)\mathcal{N}^{+}(i) contain node ii and its neighbors, and let xi​j,k(h)x_{ij,k}^{(h)} collect the applicable residuals and blending discrepancy features at layer hh. With learned coefficients αi​j​k(h)\alpha_{ijk}^{(h)}, the color update gives:

dθ,i\displaystyle d_{\theta,i} =∑h=12∑j∈𝒩+​(i)∑kαi​j​k(h)​xi​j,k(h),\displaystyle=\sum_{h=1}^{2}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{N}^{+}(i)}\sum_{k}\alpha_{ijk}^{(h)}x_{ij,k}^{(h)}, (7)
ci′\displaystyle c_{i}^{\prime} =cicf+dθ,i,hi​ℓ′=hi​ℓcf.\displaystyle=c_{i}^{\mathrm{cf}}+d_{\theta,i},\qquad h_{i\ell}^{\prime}=h_{i\ell}^{\mathrm{cf}}.

For the identity operator, all residuals and blending discrepancy features vanish, making both learned layers output zero corrections. Together with the analytic color update, this preserves the original colors by construction. The updated SH coefficients form a standard 3DGS asset with the original geometry and opacity.

4.4 Training Strategy and Objectives

Learning Aesthetic Decisions. The aesthetic enhancement network learns scene-level target operators TsT_{s} constructed from training scenes using NamedCurves (Section 3.1). To supervise the colors that determine each asset’s appearance, a color bank 𝒳s\mathcal{X}_{s} samples colors from Gaussian–viewpoint pairs according to projected footprint. The objective is:

ℒenh=13​𝔼s,x∼𝒳s​‖TΘ^s​(x)−Q8​(Ts​(x))‖1,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{enh}}=\frac{1}{3}\mathbb{E}_{s,x\sim\mathcal{X}_{s}}\|T_{\widehat{\Theta}_{s}}(x)-Q_{8}(T_{s}(x))\|_{1}, (8)

where Q8Q_{8} denotes 8-bit quantization. Training aggregates features from random input-viewpoint subsets, while inference uses all input viewpoints.

Learning Color Refinement. The color refinement network learns across scenes and target operators, with LUT interpolation and displacement scaling extending the range of photographic adjustments. Training proceeds from Gaussian-level supervision to image-level refinement. First, a rendering-based color solver initialized with the analytic color update supplies target DC corrections di⋆d_{i}^{\star}. The distillation objective is:

ℒdistill=∑iηi​‖dθ,i−di⋆‖22∑iηi,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{distill}}=\frac{\sum_{i}\eta_{i}\|d_{\theta,i}-d_{i}^{\star}\|_{2}^{2}}{\sum_{i}\eta_{i}}, (9)

where ηi\eta_{i} weights accumulated visibility. This teaches how Gaussians compensate for each other’s contributions to a target image.

Next, rendering fine-tuning aligns the predicted corrections with their effect after Gaussian blending. Reconstruction viewpoints and perturbed viewpoints expose the same edited asset to changing visibility during training. For a sampled operator TT, write the target in Eq. 1 as Is,T⋆​(v)=T⁡(Π⁡(R⁡(𝒢s,v)))I^{\star}_{s,T}(v)=T(\Pi(R(\mathcal{G}_{s},v))). The objective is:

ℒrender\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{render}} =𝔼s,T,v​[‖R⁡(𝒢s′,v)−Is,T⋆​(v)‖1]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{s,T,v}\bigl[\|R(\mathcal{G}_{s}^{\prime},v)-I^{\star}_{s,T}(v)\|_{1}\bigr] (10)
+λcorr​meani,RGB​dθ,i2,\displaystyle+\lambda_{\mathrm{corr}}\operatorname{mean}_{i,\mathrm{RGB}}d_{\theta,i}^{2},

where the image loss averages pixels and channels, and λcorr\lambda_{\mathrm{corr}} weights a penalty that keeps the learned correction close to the analytic starting point. The two networks are trained separately, with Gaussian geometry and opacity fixed throughout. The demonstration solver is detailed in Section B.4, and training configurations are provided in Appendix C.

5 Experiments and Results

5.1 Experimental Settings

Dataset and Metrics. We evaluate both tasks on all 37 scenes in ReTouch3D. The primary metric is off-trajectory Δ​E76\Delta E_{76}, which measures fidelity to the scene-consistent color target. We also report PSNR, SSIM [25], and LPIPS [31] to assess image and perceptual fidelity.

Comparison Methods. Table 1 lists the baselines used in our comparisons. To adapt reference-guided baselines to aesthetic enhancement, we use NamedCurves MIT5K-DPE [21] to generate target images from their required input views. Each baseline then applies the adjustment through its native editing pipeline. For reference-guided color transfer, all methods receive the same edited reference. Input-view counts, native output representations, and baseline adaptations are detailed in Appendix C.

Implementation Details. All experiments are conducted on a single NVIDIA RTX 5090 GPU. All training stages use AdamW [18] with OneCycle learning-rate scheduling [23]. First, we train the aesthetic enhancement network for 20,000 steps with a peak learning rate of 3×10−43\times 10^{-4}. Next, we train the blend-aware color refinement network through solver distillation for 16,000 steps with a peak learning rate of 10−310^{-3}. Finally, we apply rendering fine-tuning to the refinement network for 12,000 steps with a peak learning rate of 3×10−43\times 10^{-4}. Both tasks use a 17317^{3} grid LUT, predicted for aesthetic enhancement and fitted to the edited reference for color transfer. Full training and operator-fitting settings are in Appendices B and C.

5.2 Comparative Results

Aesthetic Color Enhancement. Table 1 shows that ReTouchGS achieves the lowest enhancement error while inferring aesthetically enhanced colors and tones directly from the asset, without running a 2D image enhancer at test time. Figure 4 illustrates this fidelity in Flowers’ foliage and Room’s warm floor and blue-green carpet, supporting asset-level prediction of photographic adjustments.

Reference-Guided Color Transfer. Table 1 shows that ReTouchGS transfers reference colors and tones to novel views with the lowest color error and LPIPS and the highest PSNR among the compared methods. Figure 5 shows preserved floor texture in Kitchen and carpet tones in Bonsai, illustrating how the shared color update combines control over appearance with scene detail preservation.

View Generalization. Held-out-view error measures color accuracy at reserved reconstruction viewpoints. The view-generalization gap is the mean off-trajectory error minus the reference-view error. Figure 6 shows consistent foliage and lawn tones across 14 held-out views of the same edited Bicycle asset. More multi-view examples appear in Section D.2. Reference-guided transfer gives similar errors of 3.81 Δ​E76\Delta E_{76} on the reference view and 3.85 on held-out views, averaged over all 37 scenes. The small off-trajectory gaps further support consistent color adjustment across viewpoints, with detailed view-wise comparisons and temporal residuals in Appendix D.

Efficiency. Table 1 shows that ReTouchGS combines compact networks with efficient editing. Its ultralight blend-aware color refinement network contains 44.7K parameters. Aesthetic color enhancement uses feed-forward prediction, while reference-guided color transfer fits 14,739 LUT values with fixed refinement weights. On an RTX 5090, median enhancement delivery takes 5.6 seconds for the DL3DV scenes and 32.8 seconds for the Mip-NeRF 360 scenes in ReTouch3D. ReTouchGS delivery times include asset loading, preparation, editing, and export. Further timing and parameter details appear in Appendices C and E.

5.3 Ablation Studies

Color Update Components. As shown in Table 2, with the grid LUT fixed, accounting for blended color context improves over direct per-Gaussian transformation, and learned refinement further improves every test scene in reference-guided transfer. This progression supports resolving how Gaussian colors blend when realizing the desired mapping.

Residual Propagation and Blending Discrepancy Features. As shown in Table 2, removing either residual propagation or blending discrepancy features reduces color accuracy and PSNR in both tasks. These results support propagating desired color changes through neighboring Gaussians and explicitly modeling their blending discrepancy.

Aesthetic Enhancement Network. Combining projected appearance and color quantiles improves operator prediction over either input alone (Appendix E). The two inputs thus provide complementary cues for predicting aesthetic color adjustments.

Additional Analysis. Appendix E shows that learned refinement improves color-mapping fidelity across seven LUT sources and that two-stage training outperforms rendering-only training. The breakdowns by scene source also show consistent transfer gains in both groups.

5.4 Adaptation to Different Retouching Targets

To evaluate whether learned color refinement transfers to a new source of photographic adjustments, we use VeraRetouch [8] to construct targets for both aesthetic color enhancement and reference-guided color transfer on all 37 scenes in ReTouch3D. The color refinement network was trained without color adjustments generated by VeraRetouch, and its weights remain fixed throughout these experiments. For aesthetic enhancement, we retrain the aesthetic enhancement network using VeraRetouch-derived labels while keeping the pretrained color refinement network fixed. For reference-guided transfer, we fit the grid LUT to the edited reference and apply the same fixed refinement network. Table 3 shows that ReTouchGS achieves the lowest color error and LPIPS and the highest PSNR and SSIM among the compared methods in both tasks. These results demonstrate that ReTouchGS adapts effectively to color adjustment labels from different retouching models while retaining a shared, fixed color refinement network, achieving higher fidelity than the compared methods in both tasks. Target construction details are in Appendix C.

6 Conclusion

We presented ReTouchGS, an ultralight framework for aesthetic color enhancement and reference-guided color transfer of pretrained 3DGS assets. Our ReTouch3D benchmark enables evaluation against scene-consistent color targets across viewpoints. Experiments show that ReTouchGS achieves lower color error than competing methods, supports efficient editing, and generalizes across viewpoints, color operators, and photographic retouching priors. These results enable practical photographic retouching of 3D assets, combining automatic aesthetic decisions with user control and geometry-preserving standard 3DGS outputs.

Appendix

Appendix A ReTouch3D Benchmark Details

A.1 Scene Assets and Statistics

Aesthetic color enhancement and reference-guided color transfer use the same 37 test assets in ReTouch3D: 28 scenes from DL3DV [17] and all nine scenes from Mip-NeRF 360 [1]. The Mip-NeRF 360 subset contains four indoor scenes, room, counter, kitchen, and bonsai, and five outdoor scenes, bicycle, flowers, garden, stump, and treehill. DL3DV assets come from the publicly released DL3DV 3DGS asset collection. We evaluate the complete assets and report supplementary breakdowns by their two scene sources. Reconstruction-viewpoint counts in Table 4 describe the full set of viewpoints supplied with each asset. Evaluation viewpoint subsets are defined in Section A.3.

Table 4 summarizes asset scale and target edit magnitude, and Table 5 provides the per-scene statistics. We render DL3DV at 960×540960\times 540 pixels and Mip-NeRF 360 at width 960 with scene-dependent heights between 622 and 640 pixels. Focal lengths scale with image dimensions, and the principal point is the image center. All renders use a black background. Edit magnitude measures the original-to-target Δ​E76\Delta E_{76} averaged over the 16 off-trajectory views within each scene. Summaries for each scene group report the mean and population standard deviation of these scene means.

A.2 Target Construction

We use pretrained NamedCurves MIT5K-DPE [21] to obtain the benchmark’s target colors and tones. Offline target construction jointly fits one scene-level color operator to the 20 input and 16 held-out reconstruction views of each scene. Source renders and enhancer outputs are clipped and quantized using:

Q8​(x)=round⁡(255​Π​(x))255,Q_{8}(x)=\frac{\operatorname{round}(255\Pi(x))}{255}, (11)

where Π\Pi clips RGB values to [0,1][0,1]. For original render II, the paired images are Q8​(I)Q_{8}(I) and Q8​(E⁡(Q8​(I)))Q_{8}(E(Q_{8}(I))), where EE denotes the pretrained image enhancer. We sample 15,000 pixel locations uniformly without replacement from each image, including background pixels. Sampling uses a fixed seed for each scene, yielding 540,000 color pairs from its 36 views.

The benchmark targets represent scene-level color and tone adjustments through a shared RGB-to-RGB mapping across viewpoints. Each scene LUT uses a uniform 17×17×1717\times 17\times 17 RGB grid with D=173=4,913D=17^{3}=4,913 LUT nodes and spacing 1/161/16. We fit LUT-node displacements from the identity mapping using the ridge objective in Section B.1, setting λLUT=10−2​tr⁡(A⊤​A)/D\lambda_{\mathrm{LUT}}=10^{-2}\operatorname{tr}(A^{\top}A)/D and solving the normal equations directly. The rows of AA contain the trilinear interpolation weights of the sampled input colors. The fitted operator interpolates the displacements, adds them to the input RGB, and clips the result to [0,1][0,1]. LUT fitting and application operate directly on rendered RGB values. Evaluation uses floating-point targets Is⋆​(v)=Ts​(Π⁡(R⁡(𝒢s,v)))I_{s}^{\star}(v)=T_{s}(\Pi(R(\mathcal{G}_{s},v))), and the edited reference image is Q8​(Is⋆​(v0))Q_{8}(I_{s}^{\star}(v_{0})). The scene LUT and target images are reserved for evaluation. Transfer methods receive the edited reference at v0v_{0}.

A.3 Viewpoint Splits

Each scene has 20 input and 16 held-out reconstruction viewpoints. DL3DV uses fixed viewpoint lists. For Mip-NeRF 360, a random permutation with seed zero assigns the first 20 reconstruction viewpoints to the input set and the next 16 to the held-out set. These sets are disjoint, and v0v_{0} is the first input viewpoint. All viewpoint lists are fixed before evaluation. The benchmark protocol records the scene identifiers, input and held-out view indices, reference view, and complete off-trajectory camera parameters. Evaluation reads the stored camera parameters directly to reproduce the same viewpoints.

We generate one off-trajectory viewpoint from each held-out viewpoint. Let tjt_{j} denote the reconstruction camera centers and t¯\bar{t} their mean. The radius rs=1.1​maxj​‖tj−t¯‖2r_{s}=1.1\max_{j}\|t_{j}-\bar{t}\|_{2} defines a sphere centered at t¯\bar{t} that encloses these centers. We sample a rotation angle uniformly from [10∘,20∘][10^{\circ},20^{\circ}] around an axis whose azimuth is uniform in [0,2​π)[0,2\pi) in the camera’s local image plane. For translation, we draw a three-dimensional standard normal vector, multiply its local depth component by 0.30.3, normalize it, and transform it to world coordinates. The translation length is 0.075​rs0.075r_{s}. Perturbations use fixed seeds for each scene and held-out viewpoint. Intrinsics and image dimensions remain fixed. The resulting 16 off-trajectory poses are reserved for evaluating the delivered asset. Together, the 20 input, 16 held-out, and 16 off-trajectory viewpoints form three evaluation groups shared by both tasks.

A.4 Metrics and Aggregation

Let I^s​(v)\hat{I}_{s}(v) denote the edited asset’s render and PvP_{v} all pixels in view vv, including the background. We clip RGB images to [0,1][0,1] and convert sRGB to CIELAB under the D65 white point [10]. The conversion uses the standard sRGB inverse transfer function and white point (Xn,Yn,Zn)=(0.95047,1,1.08883)(X_{n},Y_{n},Z_{n})=(0.95047,1,1.08883). The per-view color error is:

ds​(v)=1|Pv|​∑p∈Pv‖Lab⁡(Π​(I^s​(v))p)−Lab⁡(Is⋆​(v)p)‖2.d_{s}(v)=\frac{1}{|P_{v}|}\sum_{p\in P_{v}}\left\|\operatorname{Lab}(\Pi(\hat{I}_{s}(v))_{p})-\operatorname{Lab}(I_{s}^{\star}(v)_{p})\right\|_{2}. (12)

For an evaluation viewpoint set 𝒱s\mathcal{V}_{s}, the scene score is |𝒱s|−1​∑v∈𝒱sds​(v)|\mathcal{V}_{s}|^{-1}\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}_{s}}d_{s}(v). The overall ReTouch3D score averages all 37 scene scores equally. Breakdowns by scene source use the same equal-scene weighting within each group. The primary score uses the 16 off-trajectory viewpoints 𝒱soff\mathcal{V}_{s}^{\mathrm{off}}. The view-generalization gap is:

gs=116​∑v∈𝒱soffds​(v)−ds​(v0).g_{s}=\frac{1}{16}\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}_{s}^{\mathrm{off}}}d_{s}(v)-d_{s}(v_{0}). (13)

Both tasks use the same reference viewpoint v0v_{0}. We aggregate gsg_{s} with the same equal-scene weighting as color error.

Appendix B Method Implementation Details

B.1 Operator Fitting

The predicted enhancement LUT and the reference-fitted transfer LUT use a uniform 17317^{3} RGB grid, giving D=4,913D=4{,}913 LUT nodes storing RGB displacements and grid spacing 1/161/16. Queries use trilinear interpolation and output clipping as defined in Eq. 2. For reference-guided color transfer, the original rendering is clipped to [0,1][0,1] and paired with the edited reference pixels. The fitted displacements minimize:

Θ^=arg⁡minΘ⁡‖A​Θ−(Y−X)‖F2+λLUT​‖Θ‖F2,\widehat{\Theta}=\arg\min_{\Theta}\|A\Theta-(Y-X)\|_{F}^{2}+\lambda_{\mathrm{LUT}}\|\Theta\|_{F}^{2}, (14)

where XX and YY contain paired RGB samples and the rows of AA are the interpolation weights of XX. The identity-centered penalty anchors colors sparsely represented in the reference. Images with more than 60,000 pixels are sampled at 60,000 evenly spaced flattened indices, rounded down to integers. The ridge coefficient in Eq. 14 is λLUT=10−2​max⁡(tr⁡(A⊤​A)/D,10−9)\lambda_{\mathrm{LUT}}=10^{-2}\max(\operatorname{tr}(A^{\top}A)/D,10^{-9}). The normal equations use diagonal preconditioner diag⁡(A⊤​A)+λLUT\operatorname{diag}(A^{\top}A)+\lambda_{\mathrm{LUT}} and conjugate gradients initialized at zero. The solve stops after 80 iterations or when the joint RGB residual norm falls below 10−710^{-7}. Training labels follow the multi-view target construction in Section A.2.

B.2 Projection and Network Details

Gaussian Selection and Projection. Using the associated camera parameters 𝒞\mathcal{C}, the aesthetic enhancement network selects up to 262,144 Gaussians with the largest summed projected footprints over the 20 input viewpoints. Let ri=si(1)​si(2)r_{i}=\sqrt{s_{i}^{(1)}s_{i}^{(2)}} use Gaussian ii’s two largest scales, oio_{i} denote opacity, and di​vd_{iv} denote camera-coordinate depth at viewpoint vv. For focal length fx​vf_{xv} and grid dimensions Wv,HvW_{v},H_{v}, the footprint is:

Fi​v={min⁡(oi​(fx​v​ri/di​v)2,Wv​Hv),visible,0,otherwise.F_{iv}=\begin{cases}\min\!\left(o_{i}(f_{xv}r_{i}/d_{iv})^{2},W_{v}H_{v}\right),&\text{visible},\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (15)

A center is visible when its depth exceeds 10−310^{-3} and its projection lies inside the image. Projection grids have width 80 and preserve aspect ratio. Camera intrinsics, including the focal length used in the footprint, are scaled to this grid resolution before projection. Flooring projected coordinates assigns cell gv​(i)g_{v}(i). For visible centers, the aggregation weight is:

ωi​v=oi​exp⁡[−log⁡di​v−log⁡dv,gv​(i)min0.05],\omega_{iv}=o_{i}\exp\!\left[-\frac{\log d_{iv}-\log d^{\min}_{v,g_{v}(i)}}{0.05}\right], (16)

where dv​gmind^{\min}_{vg} is the nearest center depth in cell gg. The aesthetic enhancement network computes these weights within its selected Gaussian set.

Aesthetic Enhancement Network. A →→327\!\to\!64\!\to\!32 MLP encodes view-dependent SH RGB, opacity, and three relative log scales. The log scales subtract their median over the selected set, are sorted in descending order, clipped to [−6,6][-6,6], and divided by three. SH colors use Q8Q_{8} quantization. Training features store opacity and scales in half precision. Each cell contains the weighted feature mean, with 10−610^{-6} added to its denominator, and density channel log⁡(1+∑iωi​v)\log(1+\sum_{i}\omega_{iv}). Three convolutions map channels as →→→6433\!\to\!64\!\to\!64\!\to\!64, with kernels 3,3,13,3,1, strides 1,2,11,2,1, and padding 1,1,01,1,0. Spatial mean and maximum pooling provide 128 features. The same grid aggregates the selected Gaussians’ quantized view-dependent SH colors using ωi​v\omega_{iv}, with a 10−1210^{-12} floor on the summed-weight denominator. Occupied cells contribute equally to five quantiles: 2nd, 25th, 50th, 75th, and 98th percentiles. These quantiles of R, G, B, and luma 0.299​R+0.587​G+0.114​B0.299R+0.587G+0.114B provide 20 additional features. A →→128148\!\to\!128\!\to\!128 MLP encodes the features at each viewpoint, followed by averaging across viewpoints and a →→→32128\!\to\!128\!\to\!128\!\to\!32 coefficient head. MLP hidden layers and the first two convolutions use GELU [9]. The PCA basis has 32 columns, formed from the leading right singular vectors of the centered training-LUT matrix. For the 189 training LUTs, each coefficient standard deviation is its singular value divided by 188\sqrt{188}. The head’s final weight and bias start at zero, giving the training-LUT mean as the initial prediction.

Blended Color Context. Blended color context construction uses all Gaussians and the projection weights in Eq. 16. Let c¯j​(v)\bar{c}_{j}(v) be the view-dependent SH color clamped below at zero and Wi=∑v∈𝒞ωi​vW_{i}=\sum_{v\in\mathcal{C}}\omega_{iv}. Grid colors and blended color context are:

qv​g\displaystyle q_{vg} =∑j:gv​(j)=gωj​vc¯j(v)max(∑j:gv​(j)=gωj​v,10−12),\displaystyle=\frac{\sum_{j:g_{v}(j)=g}\omega_{jv}\bar{c}_{j}(v)}{\max(\sum_{j:g_{v}(j)=g}\omega_{jv},10^{-12})}, (17)
mi\displaystyle m_{i} ={Π⁡(∑v∈𝒞ωi​v​qv,gv​(i)Wi),Wi>10−6,ui,Wi≤10−6.\displaystyle=\begin{cases}\Pi\!\left(\dfrac{\sum_{v\in\mathcal{C}}\omega_{iv}q_{v,g_{v}(i)}}{W_{i}}\right),&W_{i}>10^{-6},\\ u_{i},&W_{i}\leq 10^{-6}.\end{cases}

B.3 Color Update Implementation

The blend-aware color refinement network in Section 4.3 predicts the DC correction dθ,id_{\theta,i} through two residual-propagation layers. Its graph connects each Gaussian to eight Euclidean nearest neighbors. Its 16-dimensional node input contains c~i\tilde{c}_{i}, mim_{i}, their difference, aia_{i}, oio_{i}, three relative log scales, log⁡(1+‖hi,ℓ>0‖F)\log(1+\|h_{i,\ell>0}\|_{F}), and log⁡(1+Wi)/3\log(1+W_{i})/3. Relative log scales use the aesthetic enhancement network’s normalization, computed over the full asset. LayerNorm and a →→6416\!\to\!64\!\to\!64 MLP encode each node. A residual context MLP with LayerNorm and widths →→64128\!\to\!64\!\to\!64 combines its embedding with the mean neighbor embedding. Both propagation layers reuse the resulting node representations, and each self head takes the corresponding 64-dimensional node embedding.

For centers pi,pjp_{i},p_{j}, the geometry channels use:

ρi​j\displaystyle\rho_{ij} =pj−pimax⁡(ri,10−6),\displaystyle=\frac{p_{j}-p_{i}}{\max(r_{i},10^{-6})}, (18)
gi​j\displaystyle g_{ij} =−‖pj−pi‖22max⁡(ri2+rj2,10−10),\displaystyle=-\frac{\|p_{j}-p_{i}\|_{2}^{2}}{\max(r_{i}^{2}+r_{j}^{2},10^{-10})},
ξi​j\displaystyle\xi_{ij} =15​[clip⁡(ρi​j,−20,20),clip⁡(gi​j,−20,0)].\displaystyle=\frac{1}{5}[\operatorname{clip}(\rho_{ij},-20,20),\operatorname{clip}(g_{ij},-20,0)].

Each edge head receives two 64-dimensional embeddings, ξi​j\xi_{ij}, and an additional copy of its clipped distance channel clip⁡(gi​j,−20,0)/5\operatorname{clip}(g_{ij},-20,0)/5, totaling 133 inputs. Self and edge heads predict the scalar coefficients that combine operator residuals and blending discrepancy features in Eq. 7. Self heads output four coefficients in the first layer and five in the second. Edge heads output five and six, respectively, including the coefficient for the edge blending discrepancy feature. All heads have 64 hidden units with GELU and zero-initialized output layers.

Let bi=bT​(ui,mi)b_{i}=b_{T}(u_{i},m_{i}), bi​j=bT​(ui,uj)b_{ij}=b_{T}(u_{i},u_{j}), and ℛi=(ridir,rictx,rijac,bi)\mathcal{R}_{i}=(r_{i}^{\mathrm{dir}},r_{i}^{\mathrm{ctx}},r_{i}^{\mathrm{jac}},b_{i}) denote the ordered residual tuple. The vectors indexed by kk in Eq. 7 are:

(xi​i,k(1))k\displaystyle(x_{ii,k}^{(1)})_{k} =ℛi,\displaystyle=\mathcal{R}_{i},
(xi​j,k(1))k\displaystyle(x_{ij,k}^{(1)})_{k} =(ℛj,bi​j),\displaystyle=(\mathcal{R}_{j},b_{ij}),
(xi​i,k(2))k\displaystyle(x_{ii,k}^{(2)})_{k} =(ℛi,di(1)),\displaystyle=(\mathcal{R}_{i},d_{i}^{(1)}),
(xi​j,k(2))k\displaystyle(x_{ij,k}^{(2)})_{k} =(ℛj,dj(1),bi​j),\displaystyle=(\mathcal{R}_{j},d_{j}^{(1)},b_{ij}),

where j∈𝒩⁡(i)j\in\mathcal{N}(i) and di(1)d_{i}^{(1)} is the first propagation layer’s correction. Parentheses concatenate the listed vectors in order. Neighbor terms use the residual vectors at node jj and are summed over the eight neighbors without normalization. The final correction sums the outputs of both layers.

The analytic color update uses δ=0.5\delta=0.5 and a boundary-adjusted central-difference Jacobian with step ϵ=1/34\epsilon=1/34. For xk±=Π⁡(x±ϵ​ek)x_{k}^{\pm}=\Pi(x\pm\epsilon e_{k}), its kkth column is (T⁡(xk+)−T⁡(xk−))/max⁡([xk+−xk−]k,10−6)(T(x_{k}^{+})-T(x_{k}^{-}))/\max([x_{k}^{+}-x_{k}^{-}]_{k},10^{-6}). The blend-aware color refinement network uses c~i=clip⁡(ci,−0.5,1.5)\tilde{c}_{i}=\operatorname{clip}(c_{i},-0.5,1.5) and JT​(mi)−I~=clip⁡(JT​(mi)−I,−5,5)\widetilde{J_{T}(m_{i})-I}=\operatorname{clip}(J_{T}(m_{i})-I,-5,5) elementwise. The analytic color update uses the original DC color and the unclipped Jacobian. The input DC color is ci=C0​hi​0+0.5c_{i}=C_{0}h_{i0}+0.5, where hi​0h_{i0} is the zeroth-order SH coefficient and C0=1/4​πC_{0}=1/\sqrt{4\pi}. After the color update, the DC SH coefficient is hi​0′=(ci′−0.5)/C0h^{\prime}_{i0}=(c_{i}^{\prime}-0.5)/C_{0}.

B.4 Solver Demonstrations

A solver demonstration provides target DC corrections for training the blend-aware color refinement network with Eq. 9. Each demonstration pairs a scene with a color operator sampled using the LUT interpolation and displacement scaling specified in Section C.1. The visibility-weighted solver of Instant Colorization [16] starts from the SH coefficients HcfH^{\mathrm{cf}} produced by the analytic color update and uses all 20 input viewpoints. Let Hi∈ℝM×3H_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times 3} contain Gaussian ii’s MM SH coefficients, and let R⁡(H,v)R(H,v) render the fixed geometry and opacity with coefficients HH. The target is Yv=T⁡(Π⁡(R⁡(𝒢,v)))Y_{v}=T(\Pi(R(\mathcal{G},v))), and the data loss is:

ℒdemo​(H)=12​∑v∈𝒞‖R⁡(H,v)−Yv‖F2.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{demo}}(H)=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{v\in\mathcal{C}}\|R(H,v)-Y_{v}\|_{F}^{2}. (19)

Appendix C Experimental Settings

C.1 ReTouchGS Training Settings

Training Data. The aesthetic enhancement network uses 189 DL3DV [17] training scenes and 23 validation scenes. Of the 189 training scenes, 145 supply the LUTs used to train the blend-aware color refinement network. Training, validation, and test scenes are disjoint. The blend-aware color refinement network uses 16 complete assets from this 145-scene subset and six validation assets, selected with seed zero. Training and validation assets contain at most 800,000 and 1,000,000 Gaussians, respectively. Each selected asset contributes all its Gaussians.

The refinement operator bank contains 580 LUTs from these 145 scenes and four pretrained enhancers: the MIT5K-DPE, PPR10K-C, and MIT5K-UEGAN variants of NamedCurves [21], and the sRGB model of image-adaptive 3D LUT [30]. Each scene-level LUT is fitted to 36 enhanced views using Section A.2. The aesthetic enhancement network learns the MIT5K-DPE targets.

Enhancement Supervision. The color bank 𝒳s\mathcal{X}_{s} in Eq. 8 contains 131,072 quantized colors per scene, sampled from pairs of Gaussians and viewpoints with replacement and probabilities proportional to Fi​vF_{iv}. Pairs are drawn from the selected Gaussian set and the 20 input viewpoints. Each entry stores the view-dependent SH color of its sampled pair, clipped to [0,1][0,1] and quantized with Q8Q_{8}. The color bank remains fixed throughout training. Each enhancement step samples four scenes with replacement and four to eight input viewpoints per scene. For each scene, the viewpoint count is sampled uniformly, and a random permutation selects the viewpoints. Each scene contributes 65,536 bank entries sampled with replacement per step. The enhancement loss averages absolute error over colors and RGB channels, including the 1/31/3 factor in the main text. Inference averages the representations from all 20 input viewpoints.

Operator Sampling and Refinement Training. During rendering fine-tuning, we sample the identity color operator with probability 0.10.1. Otherwise, we uniformly sample a bank LUT and interpolate it with another uniformly sampled bank LUT with probability 0.50.5, using a coefficient sampled from U⁡[0,1]U[0,1]. The resulting displacements are scaled by U⁡[0.5,1.5]U[0.5,1.5]. Solver demonstrations use non-identity operators drawn with the same interpolation and scaling procedure and a fixed seed per scene. Each training asset supplies 24 non-identity demonstrations, giving 384 scene-operator pairs, and each validation asset supplies eight. The solver and visibility weights for distillation are specified in Section B.4.

Both refinement stages uniformly sample a scene every four updates and reuse it for those updates. Distillation samples one solver demonstration uniformly at each update. Rendering fine-tuning draws a new operator using the sampler above. Rendering fine-tuning uses one scene, one operator, and two views per update, rendered at a width of 480 pixels. Each view uses an input camera pose with probability 0.30.3, or a perturbed pose otherwise. Perturbations use the local-axis and translation-direction construction in Section A.3, with training ranges U⁡[0∘,20∘]U[0^{\circ},20^{\circ}] for rotation and U⁡[0,0.075​rs]U[0,0.075r_{s}] for translation length. The image loss averages over sampled views, pixels, and RGB channels. The correction penalty uses λcorr=10−3\lambda_{\mathrm{corr}}=10^{-3} and averages squared corrections over Gaussians and RGB.

Optimization and Model Selection. All stages use AdamW [18], weight decay 10−410^{-4}, OneCycle [23] scheduling with 5% warm-up, and gradient-norm clipping at one. Network initialization and training-time sampling use seed zero. Aesthetic enhancement, solver distillation, and rendering fine-tuning use 20,000, 16,000, and 12,000 updates, with peak learning rates of 3×10−43\times 10^{-4}, 10−310^{-3}, and 3×10−43\times 10^{-4}, respectively. Each stage starts a new optimizer and schedule. We select the aesthetic enhancement network by mean validation image-space Δ​E76\Delta E_{76} after 5,000, 10,000, and 20,000 training updates. Validation applies the predicted and target LUTs to 20 input views per scene at width 240 and selects the model trained for 20,000 updates. Our implementation uses Python 3.10, PyTorch 2.11.0 with CUDA 12.8, and gsplat 1.5.3.

C.2 Inputs and Output Representations

All asset comparisons start from the same source assets and follow the same benchmark viewpoint protocol. In aesthetic enhancement, image-conditioned baselines obtain their targets by applying NamedCurves MIT5K-DPE [21] to input views. Instant Colorization, BilaRF, ReparamGS, FPGS, VIRGi, ViP3DE, and Omni-3DEdit receive one enhanced view, while SAAD receives sixteen. FPGS and ViP3DE also read twenty original input-view renders. ReparamGS and VIRGi use original renders for scene preparation, as detailed below. These preparation views are separate from the enhanced target images used to supervise editing. VCG is evaluated as an alternative LUT source in Section C.5. In reference-guided color transfer, each method receives the same edited image at v0v_{0}. The reference image supplies the intended color appearance for the entire scene.

We evaluate each method’s native output. Standard 3DGS assets use the common 3DGS renderer. BilaRF preserves its bilateral grid, ReparamGS preserves palette-weight SH and tone controls, and VIRGi preserves its neural color representation. Omni-3DEdit produces edited images.

C.3 Asset Editing Baselines

Instant Colorization. Instant Colorization [16] uses the authors’ color-statistics collection, visibility normalization, linear solve, and CUDA rasterizer. We provide the input Gaussian geometry and registered camera parameters, then perform the initial solve and fifty refinements from one edited view. The SH regularization weights are 10−510^{-5} for DC and 10−210^{-2} for each higher order. Each per-Gaussian system uses a direct linear solve. The output is a standard 3DGS asset.

BilaRF. We couple the authors’ CP-factorized 4D bilateral grid [24] to the input 3DGS asset to adjust colors using 3D position and learned grayscale guidance. The grid uses spatial resolution 16316^{3}, eight bins along the guidance dimension, factorization rank five, and a spatial coordinate bound of one. Its learned grayscale guidance network has width eight and depth two. Optimization uses Adam [13] for 2,500 updates, with learning rate decaying exponentially from 10−210^{-2} to 10−310^{-3}, betas (0.9,0.99)(0.9,0.99), and ϵ=10−15\epsilon=10^{-15}. The objective combines mean Charbonnier error e2+10−6\sqrt{e^{2}+10^{-6}} and the authors’ total-variation term with unit weight. Positions are normalized by the center and radius of the reconstruction camera distribution, and full-frame supervision replaces random-ray batches.

SAAD. Our implementation of SAAD [3] keeps geometry and opacity fixed and learns scene-specific appearance predictors for illumination, tone, and detail. Adam runs for 5,000 updates at learning rate 10−310^{-3}. The predictors use two hidden ReLU layers, widths 64 for illumination and tone and 32 for detail, four Fourier bands, and degree-three SH. Gaussian filters use kernel size and standard deviation (21,5)(21,5) and (7,1.5)(7,1.5). Aesthetic enhancement supplies sixteen evenly spaced enhanced views from the input set, while reference-guided color transfer supplies one edited supervision view. For numerical settings unspecified by the paper, we activate the illumination and detail branches after steps 1,000 and 3,000, respectively. The Gaussian-level auxiliary loss has weight one before the first transition and 0.10.1 afterwards. The quantile threshold for selecting detail-supervision pixels decreases from 0.950.95 to 0.700.70 after the second transition. The temperature controlling residual agreement across supervision views is 0.010.01, and DC-magnitude, direction, and higher-order-SH penalties each have weight 10−410^{-4}. Tone statistics use global and 4×44\times 4 patch means and population standard deviations in BT.601 YUV. The loss sums over pixels and supervision views, accumulating gradients from all supervision views before each update.

ReparamGS. The authors’ palette decomposition and constraint solver [4] prepare the asset for ten epochs using original renders from the reconstruction viewpoints, excluding the sixteen held-out viewpoints. Seed 42 initializes four evenly spaced chromatic palette colors, black and white, and degree-three palette-weight SH. Adam learning rates are 0.0050.005 for DC weights, 0.00050.0005 for higher orders, and 0.010.01 for palette parameters. The decomposition combines barycentric MSE, positivity with weight 0.50.5, compactness increasing from 0.0010.001 to 0.0050.005, and unit-weight hue separation with minimum gap 0.30.3. Editing uses 100 reference pixels on a fixed 10×1010\times 10 grid. The constraint solver adjusts palette colors and tone curves using damped block coordinate descent (dBCD) with iteratively reweighted least squares (IRLS). It performs up to eight outer rounds with damping 0.70.7, 100 curve samples, constraint weight weq=1,000w_{\mathrm{eq}}=1{,}000, palette-shift weight wsp=0.1w_{\mathrm{sp}}=0.1 within the sparsity term, ρ=100\rho=100, and eight inner iterations with ϵ=0.001\epsilon=0.001. The delivered representation preserves the palette and tone controls.

FPGS. FPGS [12] follows the authors’ preprocessing, feature-autoencoder training, Gaussian reconstruction, and style-transfer procedure. Twenty input-view renders provide the source images, and the input Gaussian centers and DC colors initialize the point cloud. DINO features use resolution 448, overlapping 113×113113\times 113 grids, horizontal-flip averaging, and guided filtering. The autoencoder trains for five epochs with Adam at 0.0010.001. Scene reconstruction uses 30,000 updates with RGB L1L_{1} and DSSIM, adding semantic L1L_{1} with weight 0.10.1 after step 25,000. Native densification and opacity resets are preserved. Style transfer uses two passes, temperature 100, ϵ=0.01\epsilon=0.01, and blending 0.30.3. We evaluate the resulting native 3DGS asset.

VIRGi. Our implementation of VIRGi [20] uses three-layer diffuse and specular networks of width 64, unidirectional hidden-feature connections, and a sigmoid on their summed output. The hash grid has sixteen levels with two features per level, base resolution 16, scale 1.447, and hash-table size 2192^{19}. Directions use nine degree-two SH coefficients. Preparation uses 30,000 Adam updates at learning rate 0.010.01, with 100 warm-up steps and learning-rate multipliers 0.330.33 at steps 5,000, 15,000, and 25,000. Each batch contains 32 groups of image patches, each grouping five 16×1616\times 16 patches that observe the same Gaussian from different viewpoints. The specular penalty decreases from 0.250.25 to 0.050.05. Editing updates a copy of the final diffuse layer and a soft-segmentation network for 200 steps at 0.010.01. The segmentation network predicts weights that blend the original and edited diffuse colors. Segmentation and editing settings follow IReNe [19]. Original-asset renders supervise preparation, and the native neural representation is evaluated with the source geometry and opacity.

C.4 Image Propagation Baselines

Omni-3DEdit. Omni-3DEdit [6] uses the authors’ appearance model trained for 4,000 updates and inference seed 23. For both tasks, the image-propagation pipeline receives the original/edited reference pair and sixteen off-trajectory source renders, processed in two nine-view batches with repeated views filling the final batch. VGGT-1B estimates poses from these images.

ViP3DE. ViP3DE [5] uses the authors’ custom-edit configuration. Twenty input-view renders are ordered along the capture trajectory with the reference first. For reference-guided color transfer, the supplied edited reference replaces the first-frame InstructPix2Pix edit. For aesthetic enhancement, this interface receives the output of NamedCurves on the first input view. The remaining pipeline is shared across tasks. SVD inversion and propagation use 25 steps, inversion strength 0.150.15, and internal resolution 576×1024576\times 1024. Asset fitting runs 600 Adam updates at 0.0010.001, with betas (0.9,0.99)(0.9,0.99), ϵ=10−15\epsilon=10^{-15}, seed zero, and weights ten for both L1L_{1} and perceptual losses. The native pruning and densification procedure is preserved. The input interface preserves the benchmark image dimensions and field of view, and evaluation uses the delivered 3DGS asset.

C.5 LUT Configurations and Retouching Priors

Alternative LUT Representation: GLUT. To evaluate a continuous LUT representation for reference-guided color transfer, we replace the default grid LUT with the authors’ single-LUT representation of GLUT [27], fitted to the same original/edited reference pair. It uses 32 color-space Gaussians and 716 trainable parameters, with residual connection and normalized Gaussian blending. Adam trains for twenty epochs at learning rate 0.0010.001, batch size 4,096, and seed 52, with cosine scheduling at every update and gradient clipping at one. The objective combines RGB L1L_{1}, target-chroma-weighted hue loss with weight ten, and opacity entropy with weight 0.0010.001. Following the official GLUT fitting procedure, we progressively emphasize color pairs with larger prediction errors and reuse previously selected hard samples during optimization. GLUT fits all reference pixels, whereas the grid LUT uses the sampled ridge fit in Section B.1. Both operators use the same blended color context, analytic color update, and trained blend-aware color refinement network. Table 9 compares the two LUT representations in operator accuracy and edited-asset fidelity.

Video Color Grading. Video Color Grading (VCG) [22] provides an alternative source of scene-level LUTs using the authors’ pretrained GS-Extractor and L-Diffuser. It processes twenty original input-view frames and one edited reference with 25 DDIM steps and seed 48. The edited reference corresponds to the first input viewpoint. Its native 16316^{3} LUT is sampled on a 17317^{3} grid and combined with the analytic color update for asset evaluation. Table 10 compares this LUT source with the default grid-LUT configurations in both tasks.

VeraRetouch. To evaluate generalization to a new photographic retouching prior, we construct aesthetic enhancement and reference-guided color transfer targets from VeraRetouch [8] in automatic mode with temperature zero. The blend-aware color refinement network retains its weights learned from the four enhancers in Section C.1. For aesthetic enhancement, we retrain the aesthetic enhancement network on VeraRetouch-derived scene-level LUTs. Scene-level targets and edited references follow the construction in Appendix A. The enhanced images have width 960. For reference-guided color transfer, the analytic and refined ReTouchGS variants use the same reference-fitted grid LUT. All evaluated pipelines use the same scene targets, source assets, and sixteen off-trajectory viewpoints on all 37 scenes in ReTouch3D. The reference-guided color transfer pipelines receive the same edited reference for each scene. Table 3 compares aesthetic enhancement and reference-guided color transfer under these retouching targets.

C.6 Evaluation Metrics and Statistical Analysis

PSNR uses mean squared error over all sRGB pixels and channels, with unit peak intensity and MSE floored at 10−1210^{-12}. SSIM [25] uses an 11×1111\times 11 Gaussian window with standard deviation 1.51.5, C1=0.012C_{1}=0.01^{2}, and C2=0.032C_{2}=0.03^{2}. Convolution uses valid windows, and scores average equally over window centers and RGB channels. LPIPS [31] uses AlexNet [14] and version 0.1, with RGB mapped linearly to [−1,1][-1,1]. Each metric is evaluated per view, averaged within each scene, and then averaged equally across scenes. Higher PSNR and SSIM and lower LPIPS indicate closer agreement with the scene-consistent targets.

Temporal residual measures how target-relative color error changes between corresponding scene points in adjacent views. For each view, the error field is the output’s CIELAB value minus its target’s CIELAB value at each pixel. We sort reconstruction views by image name and use the first 32 views, giving 62 directed adjacent-view pairs. Expected depth and alpha from the original asset establish the correspondences. For each direction, we reproject the destination-view error field into the source view and average the Euclidean norm of its difference from the source-view error field. Valid correspondences lie inside the destination image, have positive source depth and projected depth zz, have source and sampled destination alpha at least 0.50.5, and satisfy |z−dv′|/max⁡(z,10−6)<0.02|z-d_{v^{\prime}}|/\max(z,10^{-6})<0.02, where dv′d_{v^{\prime}} is sampled destination depth. Sampling is bilinear at pixel centers with aligned grid corners. Directions with at least 200 valid pixels contribute equally to the scene score, and scene scores contribute equally within each reported scene group. Lower temporal residual indicates more consistent target-relative color errors across views.

Statistical Analysis.

We report population standard deviations across scenes. Paired operator comparisons use 10,000 percentile-bootstrap replicates over scenes with seed zero. Each bootstrap replicate contains 37 scenes and preserves the scene-source proportions of ReTouch3D.

Appendix D Extended Experimental Results

D.1 Color and Image Fidelity

Table 6 breaks down the main asset comparisons by scene source within ReTouch3D. ReTouchGS achieves the lowest color error and LPIPS and the highest PSNR in both tasks on both source subsets of ReTouch3D. These results support accurate color reproduction across the diverse assets in ReTouch3D. Alternative LUT configurations are analyzed in Section E.2. Figures 7 and 8 extend the aesthetic enhancement comparisons to additional scenes and matched detail crops. The examples show how ReTouchGS adjusts colors and tones across vegetation, reflective surfaces, and furnished interiors while preserving scene structure. Numbers in the additional qualitative figures report mean pixelwise Δ​E76\Delta E_{76} over the displayed eight-bit image regions. All output columns within a comparison row share the same viewpoint and image region.

Figure 11 compares images edited by Omni-3DEdit [6] with renders from ReTouchGS. ReTouchGS produces coherent color changes across buildings, indoor surfaces, and small objects in this comparison. Figures 12 and 13 show reference colors reproduced across broad surfaces and fine structures in additional scenes.

D.2 Accuracy Across Viewpoint Groups

The small view-generalization gaps of ReTouchGS are accompanied by low temporal residuals in both tasks (Table 7). The latter evaluates target-relative errors at corresponding scene points, complementing the viewpoint-group comparison. These measurements support a consistent realization of the desired color adjustment across viewpoints. Figure 9 shows held-out views rendered from one enhanced asset per scene. Figure 16 extends this comparison to both tasks with five aligned held-out viewpoints per scene. The shared color update preserves the appearance of outdoor structures and indoor surfaces across viewpoints, while the matched crops relate the resulting colors directly to the target.

Appendix E Color Operator and Refinement Analysis

E.1 Color Operators and Refinement

We separate color-operator accuracy from its realization in the asset. Operator error measures how closely the input color operator’s output T⁡(Π⁡(R⁡(𝒢,v)))T(\Pi(R(\mathcal{G},v))) matches the benchmark target Is⋆​(v)I_{s}^{\star}(v). Asset error compares the edited render R⁡(𝒢′,v)R(\mathcal{G}^{\prime},v) with the same target. Operator fidelity error compares the edited render with T⁡(Π⁡(R⁡(𝒢,v)))T(\Pi(R(\mathcal{G},v))), measuring how accurately the color update realizes the input color operator. All use Δ​E76\Delta E_{76} on the sixteen off-trajectory views, averaged first within each scene and then across scenes. Table 8 compares seven grid-LUT sources with direct per-Gaussian transformation, the analytic color update, and learned refinement. For each operator source, the three color-update configurations share the operator, original asset, and viewpoints. Direct corresponds to removing blended color context and refinement in Table 2. Analytic retains the analytic color update and removes the blend-aware color refinement network. Refined adds the refinement network to the analytic color update, matching the color-update configuration of Full model in that table. The training-mean LUT is fixed across test scenes, while the aesthetic enhancement network predicts a LUT from each asset and its associated camera parameters. The image predictor reads twenty original renders, and the enhancer-based controls fit their LUTs to one, four, or twenty enhanced input views. The reference-fitted LUT uses the reference image pair.

The blend-aware color refinement network reduces operator fidelity error for all 259 scene–operator pairs across the seven operator sources in ReTouch3D. This demonstrates that the blend-aware color refinement network accurately realizes color mappings obtained through different LUT prediction and fitting procedures. Relative to the analytic color update, it also improves PSNR in 240 pairs, SSIM in 252, and LPIPS in 251. For the training-mean LUT on Mip-NeRF 360, the refined asset follows the supplied operator more closely, with operator fidelity error decreasing from 3.36 to 2.92, while its benchmark-target error changes from 10.42 to 10.52. These measurements distinguish selecting a mapping that matches the target from accurately realizing that mapping in 3D.

E.2 Alternative Color Operators

Alternative LUT Representation: GLUT. We use grid LUTs in the main experiments to maintain a consistent color-operator representation across both tasks and the color-update ablations. As a supplementary evaluation, we replace the grid LUT with GLUT [27] for reference-guided color transfer, using the same reference pair and the fitting procedures in Section C.5.

Table 9 shows that blend-aware color refinement improves all four asset metrics for both operators in both source subsets of ReTouch3D. The grid LUT has lower operator error on the DL3DV and Mip-NeRF 360 scenes, at 0.333 and 0.529 Δ​E76\Delta E_{76}, respectively, compared with 0.781 and 1.088 for GLUT. GLUT gives lower asset error with both color-update procedures, illustrating the joint role of the color mapping and Gaussian blending. Adding blend-aware color refinement to the analytic color update reduces asset error in all 37 scenes for each operator. The mean paired reduction is 0.614 Δ​E76\Delta E_{76} for the grid LUT, with a 95% confidence interval of [0.518,0.715][0.518,0.715], and 0.530 for GLUT, with [0.433,0.644][0.433,0.644]. The bootstrap procedure is specified in Section C.6. With blend-aware color refinement, GLUT improves asset error in 36 of 37 scenes relative to the grid LUT. Averaged equally over all 37 scenes, replacing the grid LUT with GLUT further reduces Δ​E76\Delta E_{76} from 4.035 to 3.829 and LPIPS from 0.0529 to 0.0480, while increasing PSNR from 29.49 to 30.04 and SSIM from 0.9221 to 0.9261. These results show that the same blend-aware color refinement network can benefit from different LUT representations.

Alternative LUT Source: VCG. Table 10 compares Video Color Grading (VCG) [22] with our default grid LUT configurations. With the analytic color update fixed, the default LUTs achieve lower color error than VCG-generated LUTs in both tasks. Adding blend-aware color refinement further improves the grid-LUT results. The LUT prediction and fitting procedures are specified in Sections C.5 and B.1.

E.3 Aesthetic Operator Prediction

To test whether spatial appearance and the overall color distribution provide complementary cues for render-free LUT prediction, we ablate the projected CNN features and color quantiles separately. We also compare with predictors driven by original renders to examine prediction accuracy across input representations and training-set sizes.

Every predictor decodes a 17317^{3} LUT from 32 PCA coefficients using a basis fitted to its own training targets. Image predictors read twenty original renders at width 240. Variants of the aesthetic enhancement network construct width-80 projection grids directly from Gaussian attributes and associated camera parameters. The projected-CNN variant omits the color quantiles, and the quantile-only variant zeros the pooled CNN features. The combined network concatenates both inputs.

All variants follow the aesthetic enhancement network’s optimization and model-selection settings in Section C.1. Image predictors sample four to twenty views per training scene and supervise image pixels. Aesthetic enhancement network variants sample four to eight viewpoints and use the color bank 𝒳s\mathcal{X}_{s} for supervision. The 36- and 72-scene training sets are nested subsets of the 145-scene training set, sampled with seed zero. The 189-scene training set contains these 145 scenes and 44 further scenes.

Table 11 measures operator error by comparing predicted and target LUT outputs on the same original renders. Validation uses twenty input views at width 240 per scene. Testing samples 30,000 pixels from each of sixteen native-resolution held-out views per scene. For NamedCurves [21], combining projected appearance and color quantiles improves both validation and held-out-view prediction over either input alone. Increasing the training set to 189 scenes improves validation error for both retouching priors.

At matched training-set sizes, image predictors achieve lower operator error (Table 11). This advantage is consistent with their access to rendered appearance, which explicitly captures visibility and blended pixel colors. Our aesthetic enhancement network summarizes scene appearance through coarse Gaussian projections and color quantiles, enabling direct prediction from the asset without rendering input images. Both predictor types learn the retouching prior during training and require no test-time image-enhancer calls. The comparison reflects their respective input representations, resolutions, and supervision schemes.

E.4 Refinement Mechanisms and Training

The refinement mechanism ablations on all 37 scenes share training scenes, solver demonstrations, and rendering fine-tuning steps. The residual-propagation ablation removes cross-Gaussian residual contributions and edge blending discrepancy contributions while retaining self residual updates and neighbor feature aggregation. Table 12 breaks down the scene-weighted means in Table 2 by scene source. Figures 14 and 15 isolate the local effects of residual propagation and blending discrepancy features in the two tasks. All variants use the same grid LUT and viewpoint. The matched crops and error maps show that both mechanisms reduce local color deviations around reflective details and thin foliage, connecting the aggregate gains to spatially localized corrections.

The training-strategy comparison uses six validation scenes and four operators per scene from NamedCurves [21] MIT5K-DPE, PPR10K-C, MIT5K-UEGAN, and image-adaptive 3D LUT [30]. Each scene score averages its four operators before computing the mean and population standard deviation across scenes. We compare two-stage training with rendering-only training at matched rendering and total update budgets. Rendering-only training uses either 12,000 updates to match the rendering budget or 28,000 updates to match the total training budget. Solver distillation and rendering-only training use a peak learning rate of 10−310^{-3}. The rendering fine-tuning stage uses 3×10−43\times 10^{-4}. Two-stage training achieves 2.629±0.5302.629\pm 0.530 Δ​E76\Delta E_{76}, compared with 2.666±0.5422.666\pm 0.542 for 12,000 rendering-only updates and 2.657±0.5412.657\pm 0.541 for 28,000 updates. It improves over the matched-total-budget alternative in all six scenes, supporting solver distillation as an effective initialization for rendering fine-tuning.

E.5 Target and Visibility Analysis

Scene-Consistent and Per-View Targets. We also evaluate edited assets against NamedCurves [21] outputs produced independently at each off-trajectory viewpoint. The enhancer receives the original render quantized to eight bits, and its output is quantized to eight bits for scoring. Table 13 uses the grid-LUT configuration for both tasks, holding each input operator fixed across color-update procedures. Blend-aware color refinement improves mean accuracy under both target definitions for both tasks in both source subsets of ReTouch3D. The per-view targets include the image enhancer’s view-dependent adjustments, while the scene-consistent targets evaluate consistent colors and tones throughout the asset.

Regions Beyond the Input Views. We identify Gaussians whose accumulated rendered compositing weight over the twenty input viewpoints is below 10−610^{-6}. At each off-trajectory viewpoint, we select foreground pixels with accumulated alpha above 0.5 for which these Gaussians contribute more than half of that alpha. The selected pixels occupy 2.37% of the pooled foreground on DL3DV and 4.43% on Mip-NeRF 360. The masks come from the original asset and remain fixed across methods. Table 13 pools color-error sums and selected-pixel counts across views and scenes. Learned refinement improves over the analytic color update in all four settings, supporting color transfer into regions weakly covered by the input views.

E.6 Rendering Requirements

We compare rendering requirements during asset preparation and editing. Starting from a pretrained 3DGS asset, image-conditioned enhancement baselines render source views to construct their targets. BilaRF [24], SAAD [3], and Instant Colorization [16] also use rendered supervision during editing. ReparamGS [4], FPGS [12], and VIRGi [20] render views for scene-specific preparation. ViP3DE [5] and Omni-3DEdit [6] propagate edits through source images, while VCG [22] uses an input-view sequence to predict its LUT. In contrast, ReTouchGS predicts the scene-level color operator with its aesthetic enhancement network and applies the render-free color update directly to the asset. Reference-guided color transfer renders the original reference view once for paired operator fitting, followed by the same render-free color update.

E.7 Computational Cost

Execution Time and Parameter Counts. Table 14 summarizes mean execution time, network parameters, and scene-specific optimization variables over all 37 scenes.

Execution time in Tables 1 and 14 includes asset loading, editing, and native-output export, measured with synchronized GPU boundaries, with the method-specific scopes below. Image-target generation, evaluation, and preview rendering are timed separately. ReparamGS, FPGS, and VIRGi include scene preparation for enhancement and reuse it for transfer. All methods are run on a single NVIDIA RTX 5090 GPU with 32 GB memory.

ViP3DE enhancement includes input preparation and editing. Its transfer interval includes model loading, propagation, asset fitting, validation, and export, with source rendering and input preparation performed beforehand. Omni-3DEdit includes input preparation and two image-propagation batches, with source rendering and global model initialization performed beforehand. First-use initialization is included when it occurs. GLUT times cover fitting, context preparation, and color update.

Network parameter counts include each instantiated model component once, including frozen modules and the NamedCurves enhancer used by image-conditioned enhancement baselines. For GLUT, they include the 716 parameters of its Gaussian LUT representation. Scene variables count quantities optimized or solved during preparation and editing, averaged across scenes when their size depends on the Gaussian population. Prep. vars. and Edit vars. distinguish one-time scene preparation from optimization for a particular edit. These counts describe different aspects of a method: a scene-trained network contributes to both, while a direct color solve contributes only scene variables. Methods with zero network parameters use analytic color updates or direct optimization of scene-specific color variables. Network parameter counts exclude fixed Gaussian storage, optimizer state, and evaluation models. The grid LUT used for transfer has 14,739 fitted values. Aesthetic enhancement predicts its LUT with no per-scene optimization.

Preparation-Inclusive Delivery. Table 16 reports median delivery times on the RTX 5090, including asset loading, scene preparation, editing, and export. When preparation is reused, its original computation time is included to represent delivery of the first edit.

Color-Update Components. Component times in Table 16 measure fitting, context preparation, and color updates separately. Grid fitting uses a GPU-synchronized solver interval. GLUT fitting includes optimization, validation, and parameter export. Total update sums the analytic color update and blend-aware color refinement, while delivery times additionally include asset loading and export.
